To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the R$^*$$^*$$^*$-tree, a space-time extension to the R$^+$-tree, is a versatile index that supports queries on the spatiotemporal extents of entities, that it can be tuned to prioritize space versus time in a query, and that it outperforms the R$^+$$^+$-tree and the R$^-$-tree in most cases.
the index supports the full spectrum of spatial and temporal query types and is efficient on both spatially and temporably restrictive queries.

the proposed index is the first to support both valid and transaction time and to support now, that it is the first to provide a means of prioritizing spatial versus temporal aspects of a query, and that it provides a versatile and efficient index for spatio-temporal databases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the indexing of now-relative spatiotemporal data.
the indexing of spatio-temporally referenced data.
a spatio-temporal index that supports queries that are spatially or temporally restrictive, or both, and that can adapt to the relative importance of space and time.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this is the first index that can be applied in a wide variety of spatio-temporally restrictive applications.
the spatio-temporally extended R$^*$tree is the first index to efficiently support a general class of now-relative spatiotemporal queries.
the index is efficient for a wide class of spatial queries, and for queries that restrict space or time, it is efficient in comparison with existing spatio-temporal indices.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed the first efficient and general index for spatio-bitemporal data.
this paper presents the first spatio-temporal index that supports both valid time and transaction time and that is based on the well-known R$^*$ tree.
we have developed the first efficient index for spatio-temporal objects with a spatial extent that changes discretely.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatio-temporality of data is best handled by a single, integrated index that supports the special properties of both time and space.
spatio-temporal indexing should be based on an index for the temporal dimension, with spatial dimensions added as needed.
spatio-temporal indexing can be done without sacrificing the efficiency and versatility of either spatial or temporal indexing.
